section.md: \text{What is one small piece, and what does it contribute?}
section.p: That is the main skill of applications of integration.

subsection.title: Skills: choose the small piece
subsection.p: The hardest step is usually not the antiderivative. The hardest step is choosing what to add.
A useful setup routine is:

li.p: Decide what quantity is being measured: area, volume, mass, work, force, probability, length, or surface area.
Choose a slicing variable: usually x, y, or time t.
Draw or describe one typical small piece.
Write the contribution of that piece.
Find the limits of accumulation.
Check units and signs.

subsection.p: The unit check is often the best error detector.
For example, if a work integral has units
then the integrand should contain a force times a distance. If a hydrostatic force integral has units
then the integrand should contain pressure times area.

note.title: What the project tests
note.p: The disk, washer, and shell methods are not separate tricks. They are different ways of choosing the small piece. A good method is the one that makes the small piece easy to describe.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: This chapter has shown why integrals matter.
They measure area, volume, mass, center of mass, work, hydrostatic force, average value, probability, arc length, and surface area.
But setting up an integral is not the same as evaluating it.
Even simple applications can produce integrals such as

Substitution will not handle all of these. Some require reversing the product rule. Some require trigonometric identities. Some require a clever triangle. Some require partial fractions. Some have no elementary antiderivative at all.
That is the next problem.

note.p: The small piece tells us what to integrate. Now we need better ways to integrate it.

subsection.p: The next chapter develops techniques for finding antiderivatives when substitution alone is not enough.
